frontSheet: This is a self-assessment of an estate you already run, not a procurement scoring. The EC Cloud Sovereignty Framework is its reference, never a conformance target.

Expected ceiling: no real estate reaches SEAL-3 today, because chips plus hardware supply chains are not EU-controlled — the EC's own lessons-learnt say the same. The working range is SEAL-0 to SEAL-2, so a 2 is an achievement, not a shortfall.
Don't know is an honest answer. It never counts as zero; the floor is always reported together with its unknown count, so a guess is worse than an admission.

Pre-work (see csf-prework.md): bring contract summaries — continuity, escrow, audit clauses — from the contracts desk, plus energy, facility-operator data from estates management. Six questions lean on them.

sealLevels.name: No Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: No sovereign control; fully dependent on a foreign-controlled provider.

sealLevels.name: Jurisdictional Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: Operated under EU jurisdiction, but control can still be overridden from outside.

sealLevels.name: Data Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: The EU controls the data even under stress; outside parties cannot compel access.

sealLevels.name: Technological Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: The EU controls the technology and can keep operating if a foreign supplier withdraws.

sealLevels.name: Full Digital Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: Complete sovereign control across law, data, and technology, down to the supply chain.

roles.name: Architecture
roles.description: Designs the estate; owns topology and platform choices.

roles.name: Platform ops
roles.description: Runs the estate day to day.

roles.name: Security
roles.description: Owns controls, identity, and incident response.

roles.name: Legal
roles.description: Owns contracts, jurisdiction, and data-protection law.

roles.name: Procurement
roles.description: Owns supplier selection, exit, and commercial terms.

roles.name: Facilities/ESG
roles.description: Owns data-centre siting, power, and sustainability.

parties.name: Institution
parties.description: The assessed party — the estate owner (EC: Contracting Authority).

parties.name: Subprocessor
parties.description: A legal entity involved in delivery of the contract.

questions.text: Where does ultimate authority over this provider's decisions that affect your estate — pricing, roadmap, whether service continues — finally reside?
questions.why: Under stress, the provider does what its controlling entity decides; sovereignty starts with where that decision would actually be made.

ladder.description: A non-EU parent or head office makes, or can override, every material decision about this provider's service to you.
An EU-registered entity signs your contracts, but pricing, roadmap or continuation decisions can be overridden from outside the EU.
Day-to-day authority sits with an EU entity under ring-fenced governance; strategy or financing still traces to a non-EU owner.
The provider is EU-domiciled and makes its decisions in the EU/EEA; no outside veto exists over service to your estate.
Decisive authority and financing are fully vested in EU/EEA entities across the whole ownership chain, verifiable from public registers.

questions.text: If this provider were acquired, merged or made insolvent, which of your contractual protections — continuity clauses, escrow, assignment consent — would survive?
questions.why: An acquisition can move your provider under foreign control overnight; only rights that survive the change of ownership still protect you the morning after.

ladder.description: No such protections exist in the signed contracts, or nobody present can say whether they do.
Assurances are informal or draft-stage; nothing enforceable survives a change of control.
The signed contract for the core service carries continuity or escrow clauses; coverage of the remaining services is unknown.
Enforceable continuity, escrow and assignment-consent clauses cover every service you take from this provider.
Those clauses are proven exercisable: escrow releases have been tested and legal review confirms they bind a successor.

questions.text: If a non-EU authority ordered this provider to suspend or degrade your service, what would still run — for how long?
questions.why: The EC anchors sovereignty levels in what survives a break in access, not in how well the programme runs on a good day.

ladder.description: Operations dependent on this provider stop almost immediately; no bridging capability exists.
A paper plan exists; it has never been exercised, so the real bridging window is unknown.
Tested mitigations cover the highest-risk workloads — offline operation, local copies, escrowed artifacts — buying days to weeks.
A tested bridging arrangement keeps the full estate running for a defined window of 90 days or more.
Operations continue indefinitely without this provider; the dependency is fully substitutable.

questions.text: Which national legal system governs your contract with this provider — before which courts could you actually enforce a judgment?
questions.why: When a dispute or compelled act lands, the governing law plus the practically reachable court decide whether your rights exist anywhere but on paper.

ladder.description: A non-EU legal system governs the contract; disputes sit before non-EU courts or arbitration.
An EU governing-law clause exists, but the counterparty holds no EU assets a judgment could reach.
EU member-state law governs; enforcement would run against a thin EU subsidiary of a non-EU group.
EU law and exclusive EU venue govern; the provider holds substantial EU assets a judgment can reach.
Exclusive EU jurisdiction end to end, with enforcement proven or uncontested against an EU-anchored counterparty.

questions.text: Could a non-EU government compel this provider — or anyone in its corporate chain — to hand over your data?
questions.why: Who can lawfully compel disclosure is the sovereignty fact itself; encryption and residency only matter within its reach.

ladder.description: The provider is directly subject to extraterritorial disclosure law — US CLOUD Act, FISA 702, Chinese NIL or equivalent.
Reach arrives via a parent or affiliate; the contract promises notice where lawful — a promise a gag order overrides.
The operating entity is EU-incorporated with separated operations; ownership still ties it to a non-EU group.
Every entity in the ownership chain is EU/EEA-domiciled; no non-EU parent exists to receive an order.
The whole chain, subprocessors included, is verified free of any extraterritorial nexus — today an aspiration; see the front sheet.

questions.text: Does this provider hold standing technical means — privileged accounts, remote support channels, escrowed keys, update push — that could reach your systems without your action?
questions.why: A channel that works without you is the path a compelled provider would use, under a gag order you would never see.

ladder.description: Standing privileged channels exist, and the provider sits where a gag order could silence any warning to you.
Standing channels exist under non-EU reach; contractual notice is promised where the law allows it.
Standing channels exist, but the provider answers to EU jurisdiction only — no foreign gag can attach to them.
No standing access: every provider intervention requires your per-incident approval and is logged on your side.
Access without your keys and your people is technically impossible, and that design has been independently verified.

questions.text: Could a foreign export-control or sanctions decision lawfully revoke, suspend or restrict the licences or subscriptions this provider supplies you?
questions.why: Sanctions exposure is a switch someone else holds; the question measures the reach of that switch, not your paperwork about it.

ladder.description: Yes — the licences sit directly under a foreign regime such as US EAR or OFAC, revocable at source.
Exposure arrives indirectly, through the provider's corporate family or re-export conditions on components.
Direct licences are out of foreign reach; a residual exposure remains via upstream inputs the provider itself buys.
Nothing this provider supplies you sits under a foreign export-control or sanctions regime.
The full supply chain behind this provider is verified free of foreign export-control reach — today an aspiration; see the front sheet.

questions.text: Does this provider disclose — publicly or to you — the government demands for customer data it receives?
questions.why: Disclosure practice never changes who can compel the provider, so it informs the picture without setting the floor; it is how you would learn the pressure exists.

ladder.description: No transparency reporting exists, and no contractual duty to tell you about government demands.
General claims are published; nothing is verifiable, itemised or committed to you.
Transparency reporting is published on a recurring schedule; you hold no contractual notification right.
Verified reporting, plus a contractual commitment to notify you of demands where legally possible.
Verified reporting, institution-specific notification, and a commitment to challenge overbroad demands in court.

questions.text: For this dimension, who holds the cryptographic keys — could any outside party reach plaintext without your action?
questions.why: Whoever holds the keys decides, under stress, whether data is protected or merely stored; custody is the control fact the encryption paperwork stands on.

ladder.description: Keys are generated and held by the provider; plaintext is technically reachable without you.
Provider-held keys under contractual restrictions; the technical path to plaintext remains theirs.
You control the keys, but they live in a non-EU-controlled key-management service.
Keys sit in EU-jurisdiction HSMs under your control; a provider support path to them still exists.
Custody is exclusively yours: keys are generated, stored and used where no other party can touch them, by design.

questions.text: Is every place this dimension stores, processes or replicates your data — disaster recovery included — inside EU/EEA territory?
questions.why: Territory decides which courts can reach the data at rest; a non-EU fallback path is a standing invitation for the day you least want it.

ladder.description: Routine storage or processing happens outside the EU/EEA today.
Primary operations are in the EU; disaster-recovery or overflow paths leave it.
All territory is EU/EEA, but a non-EU entity operates the underlying service.
EU territory with EU operators; the remaining non-EU technical touchpoints — firmware, telemetry — are documented.
No non-EU path exists under any operating condition, emergencies included.

questions.text: Who operates the physical facilities beneath this estate — building access, power, cooling?
questions.why: Physical access sits beneath every software control; a foreign-run building is a gap no layer above it can close.

ladder.description: A non-EU-controlled operator runs the facilities; access terms are not fully known.
A non-EU operator runs them under an EU-law colocation contract.
An EU operator runs them; its ownership or maintenance chain traces outside the EU.
EU-operated under EU control; the non-EU dependencies that remain — parts, service visits — are documented and escorted.
Wholly EU-operated and EU-controlled, maintenance chain included.

questions.text: Who controls the AI models this estate runs in production — could you redeploy them without the original vendor?
questions.why: A model you cannot re-host is a service someone else can switch off; weights plus infrastructure decide whether AI is yours or borrowed.

ladder.description: Models are reached only through closed non-EU vendor APIs; no weight access, no redeployment right.
Rights to obtain weights exist on paper; they have never been obtained or exercised.
Weights are held under a vendor-gated licence; redeployment is legally possible but untested.
Models run on infrastructure you control, or redeployment without the vendor has been tested end to end.
Models and serving infrastructure are EU-controlled; vendor withdrawal has been demonstrated survivable.

questions.text: Do prompts, documents or outputs sent to AI services ever train or improve models outside your control?
questions.why: Data that trains someone else's model has left your control permanently; no deletion request reaches inside the weights.

ladder.description: Provider terms allow training on your inputs; no restriction is in place.
An opt-out is claimed; nothing verifies it.
Training is contractually disabled for the named services; you rely on the provider's attestation.
Training is technically disabled and verified — by audit, or by an architecture that keeps inputs inside your boundary.
Processing never leaves institution-controlled infrastructure; there is no vendor to leak to.

questions.text: When you delete data, can you verify no recoverable copy remains — backups, caches, derived artifacts included?
questions.why: Deletion you cannot verify is a request, not a control; under stress the copies you forgot are the ones that surface.

ladder.description: No deletion process exists beyond the provider's defaults.
Deletion requests are submitted; the provider's attestation is the only assurance.
Deletion is verified for primary storage; backups and derived artifacts rest on attestations.
Deletion is independently verifiable across primary storage, backups and derived artifacts.
Customer-held-key crypto-shredding makes every copy unreadable without your keys, backed by contractual audit rights on residual data.

questions.text: Could this dimension's workloads re-host onto a different provider or distribution without a rewrite — on open formats, open interfaces?
questions.why: Portability is the exit everything else prices against; proprietary interfaces are the lock that turns a supplier into a landlord.

ladder.description: Re-hosting means a rewrite; proprietary formats and interfaces carry the core workloads.
Standard interfaces exist, but proprietary extensions are load-bearing for core functions.
Workloads are portable except named proprietary dependencies, each with a documented workaround.
Open formats and publicly governed interfaces end to end; portability is designed but unproven.
Proven: an end-to-end migration to an alternate platform ran within the last 24 months.

questions.text: Do your engineers hold the source code, configuration baselines, operational documentation needed to understand, troubleshoot, modify this dimension?
questions.why: When the vendor is gone or gagged, what your engineers can open and read is the entire remaining support organisation.

ladder.description: Nothing beyond user-facing manuals is accessible.
Operational configurations are documented in-house; source stays closed.
Source is readable for the core components; build knowledge and modification knowledge are missing.
Source, configurations and operational documentation are held for every component except a named list of exceptions.
Full access, exercised: your engineers routinely troubleshoot and modify from source.

questions.text: Could EU-resident, EU-employed staff operate, troubleshoot, evolve this estate without offshore engineers?
questions.why: Support withdrawal is survivable exactly as far as the people inside EU jurisdiction can carry the stack alone.

ladder.description: Day-to-day operation depends on non-EU vendor engineers.
EU staff operate the estate; troubleshooting beyond runbooks needs offshore support.
EU-resident staff operate and troubleshoot; evolution — upgrades, architecture — still needs the vendor.
EU-resident, EU-employed staff cover operating, troubleshooting and evolving; single-person dependencies are documented.
Full-stack capability is in-house and redundant across people.

questions.text: Can your team build, test, deploy fixes for this dimension on its own schedule — without waiting for a non-EU party's code or approval?
questions.why: Whoever gates your patches owns your exposure window; under an active exploit, waiting is the vulnerability.

ladder.description: Every fix is authored and shipped by a non-EU vendor on its own schedule; you wait, then apply.
A support contract lets you expedite, but the vendor still authors every fix.
Your team backports or hot-fixes named components; the rest wait for the vendor.
Your team, or a contracted EU party, can author, build and deploy fixes across the dimension; no outside approval can hold them.
Self-patching is routine; vendor involvement is optional end to end.

questions.text: Are this provider's support, escalation, managed-service personnel restricted to EU jurisdiction by contract?
questions.why: Support sessions are privileged access by another name; the jurisdiction of the person on the other end is part of your attack surface.

ladder.description: Support runs from non-EU jurisdictions with no restriction.
EU preference is stated; nothing enforces it.
Routine support is contractually EU-only; emergency escalation still reaches non-EU teams.
EU-only support and escalation, contractually; exceptions need your written consent per case.
EU-only is guaranteed and legally analysed: no foreign law can compel an override.

questions.text: Would this dimension keep running if its external chokepoint — licence server, activation check, update channel, CDN, DNS — went dark or refused you?
questions.why: A dependency that phones home is a switch in someone else's hand; the EC's level idiom asks what still works when it flips.

ladder.description: A hard dependency exists; the dimension halts or degrades within days of a cut-off, with no fallback.
The dependency is known; grace periods and fallbacks have never been established.
A documented grace period or fallback covers the highest-risk components; none of it has been tested.
Fallbacks are tested: the dimension survives a cut-off with documented, bounded degradation.
No external chokepoint exists for this dimension.

questions.text: Is there a documented continuity plan for loss of vendor support, key people or supply — how recently was it tested?
questions.why: A plan is preparation, not control — it informs the picture without setting the floor; the suspension questions grade what would actually still run.

ladder.description: No documented continuity plan exists.
A plan is documented; it has never been tested.
Tabletop-tested; findings remain open.
Tested within the last 12 months; findings are tracked to closure.
Live or full-scale exercise within the last 12 months; every finding closed.

questions.text: How far does this dimension's critical path run on non-EU proprietary technology that could not be substituted?
questions.why: Unsubstitutable foreign components are the load-bearing walls someone else owns; everything above them is decor.

ladder.description: The critical path is built on non-EU proprietary technology throughout.
Open or EU alternatives exist in places; the spine remains non-EU proprietary.
Reliance is quantified and bounded: the non-EU proprietary components are named, with substitution candidates identified.
Non-EU proprietary reliance is the exception — each instance known, documented, with an exit path.
None: the critical path runs entirely on technology the EU sphere controls or can fork.

questions.text: Do you know the origin — designer, maker, jurisdiction — of the hardware, firmware, embedded code beneath this dimension?
questions.why: You cannot de-risk silicon you have never traced; provenance knowledge is where every hardware sovereignty decision starts, and the ceiling the front sheet declares lives here.

ladder.description: Provenance of hardware, firmware and embedded code is unknown, untracked.
Vendor-level knowledge only: you know whose badge is on the box, not what is inside it.
The highest-risk systems are traced to component level; jurisdictions of origin are identified.
Provenance is tracked and de-risking has begun: diversified sourcing, open-ISA pilots, EU-designed options where they exist.
Verified EU or open provenance — or audited substitutability — across the dimension. Unreachable today; see the front sheet.

questions.text: Under whose jurisdiction do the entities that develop, package, distribute, sign this dimension's software operate?
questions.why: The pipeline that builds your software can be compelled like any other operator — each stage is a hand on your future code.

ladder.description: Every stage of the pipeline operates under non-EU jurisdiction.
Contracts reference EU terms; the pipeline entities themselves remain non-EU.
Build stages run under EU jurisdiction; signing or distribution still sits outside it.
All stages operate under EU jurisdiction; the remaining non-EU touchpoints are documented.
The entire pipeline operates exclusively under EU jurisdiction.

questions.text: Who signs the software artifacts, updates, firmware this estate runs — in which jurisdiction do those signing keys live?
questions.why: Whoever signs your updates decides what you will be running next month; signing custody is control over your future state.

ladder.description: Non-EU vendors sign everything; you verify nothing on arrival.
Non-EU vendors sign; you verify integrity against their manifests.
EU-jurisdiction vendors sign the operating core; the non-EU-signed remainder is listed.
EU-held keys sign everything you build or redistribute; third-party components carry EU-vendor signatures except documented exceptions.
Institution- or EU-controlled signing end to end, with keys generated and held in EU jurisdiction.

questions.text: Do your contracts give you — or an EU auditor acting for you — an enforceable right to audit this provider's supply chain, sub-suppliers included?
questions.why: Without an audit right, the supply chain is whatever the vendor says it is; the right to look is itself the control.

ladder.description: No audit right exists; vendor self-attestation is all you hold.
The direct contract is auditable; sub-suppliers are out of reach.
Tiered audit rights exist on paper; none has been exercised.
Audit rights have been exercised within the current contract cycle; findings are tracked.
Unconditional tiered audit rights for you or an EU auditor, exercised on schedule.

questions.text: What do the licences beneath this dimension legally let you do without vendor consent — inspect, modify, fork, redistribute?
questions.why: The licence is the sovereignty you keep when goodwill runs out: a fork right needs no seat at anyone's table.

ladder.description: Closed licences throughout; no right to inspect or modify anything load-bearing.
Open components exist; the load-bearing pieces remain closed.
The core runs open-licensed; closed components persist inside the critical path.
Full open-source rights across the critical path, except named closed exceptions with exit plans.
Every component carries an unconditional right to inspect, modify, fork and continue.

questions.text: Have you costed — then actually drilled — the exit from this dimension's highest-risk component?
questions.why: An exit that was never priced or rehearsed is a hope; the drill is what converts it into a capability the minimum rule can trust.

ladder.description: No exit has been costed for any component.
Exit options are identified; none is costed or tested.
Exits are costed for the highest-risk components; no drill has run.
One full migration drill has run for the highest-risk component, data conversion included.
Every critical component holds a costed exit; the highest-risk one has been drilled end to end.

questions.text: If upstream build infrastructure vanished tomorrow, could you — or a contracted EU party — build this dimension's critical components from source?
questions.why: An estate that cannot build is controlled by whoever can; independent build capability is the deepest technical control there is.

ladder.description: Never attempted: the estate consumes vendor binaries only.
Build instructions and sources are collected; no independent build has succeeded.
At least one critical component has been built independently, end to end, on EU-controlled infrastructure.
More than half the critical components rebuild reproducibly on EU-controlled infrastructure, with an EU mirror of the dependencies relied on operationally.
End-to-end independent build capability, exercised as routine.

questions.text: Does the institution — directly or via EU bodies — carry weight in the communities that steward its critical dependencies?
questions.why: Influence upstream is early warning plus a voice in the roadmap — leverage worth recording, though it changes nothing about who controls what is deployed, so it never sets the floor.

ladder.description: Pure consumer: no engagement with the communities behind your critical dependencies.
Sporadic engagement — bug reports, self-interested fixes — with no sustained presence.
Sustained contribution or funded membership in at least one critical community.
Maintainer or steering roles held in one or more critical dependencies.
Resourced influence across the critical dependencies: seats, maintainers, funding.

questions.text: Where are the people who staff your security operations — employed, contracted, physically located?
questions.why: Your defenders can be compelled too; the jurisdiction that employs your SOC decides whose orders it must follow under stress.

ladder.description: Security operations are outsourced to a non-EU entity with non-EU staff.
EU-located staff, employed by a non-EU entity.
An EU subsidiary employs the staff; tooling and escalation run through a non-EU parent SOC.
An EU entity with EU staff; non-EU partners advise without operational access.
Fully EU: employment, contracts, location and escalation paths.

questions.text: In which jurisdiction do your security telemetry, SIEM data, audit logs live — who administers the tooling holding them?
questions.why: Telemetry maps your defences; whoever holds or administers it can be compelled to blind you, or to hand the map to someone else.

ladder.description: A non-EU SaaS holds the telemetry; non-EU staff administer it.
Data sits in an EU region of a non-EU-controlled service.
EU storage; a non-EU-controlled operator administers the tooling — support backdoors, shared key management.
EU storage under EU-controlled administration; remaining non-EU touchpoints are documented.
EU end to end: storage, administration, keys and support.

questions.text: Who controls the identity root that authenticates every login to this estate — could an outside party disable or impersonate access?
questions.why: The identity root is the estate's master switch: whoever controls it can lock every door or open any of them, without touching a single server.

ladder.description: The identity root is a non-EU-controlled service; a foreign order could cut or impersonate every login.
Non-EU identity software runs institution-hosted; updates and licensing remain a foreign gate.
An EU-jurisdiction identity service, or self-hosted open software whose recovery depends on one external party.
An institution-controlled identity root on open software; federation dependencies are documented and revocable.
EU-controlled end to end: no outside party can disable, impersonate or lock out access.

questions.text: Which non-EU-based people could obtain privileged access to this dimension's systems — under whose approval, with what trace?
questions.why: Privileged sessions are where compelled access would land in practice; who approves them, plus who sees them, is the governance that survives an order.

ladder.description: Standing privileged access exists for vendor or parent staff — neither logged nor time-bound.
Sessions are logged after the fact; approval sits with the vendor.
Time-bound sessions the vendor approves; your side receives the logs.
Case-by-case, institution-approved sessions — time-bound, fully logged on your side.
No non-EU privileged access is possible: no credentials exist, no remote channel reaches these systems.

questions.text: Can you — or an EU regulator acting for you — audit this provider's service to full depth, on demand, without vendor mediation?
questions.why: A right to look, exercised at will, is enforceable control; certificates only report what someone else saw last year.

ladder.description: No independent audit right; vendor attestations are the only view inside.
Audits happen on the vendor's terms: scope, timing and personnel are theirs to set.
Independent audits are possible with named exclusions — shared infrastructure, third-party facilities.
A full-access right is guaranteed, and it has been exercised at least once.
Unconditional, on-demand, full-depth audit for you or an EU regulator, with no mediation.

questions.text: Which security certifications cover this provider's operating entity — general schemes or EU sovereign ones?
questions.why: A certificate attests controls, it is not the controls — recorded here as the most verifiable evidence in the file, never as the floor.

ladder.description: None — or the only certificate names an affiliate that is not the operating entity.
A general scheme of the ISO 27001 class covers the group, not the operating entity.
A general scheme covers the operating entity for this estate's scope.
An EU scheme — C5, SecNumCloud, EUCS-class — covers the operating entity for this scope.
An EU sovereign-tier scheme at its highest level, current, scoped to the operating entity.

questions.text: Does the institution measure, publish, improve the environmental footprint of this estate — energy, hardware lifecycle, efficiency?
questions.why: Environmental facts move no sovereignty floor — the EC's own architecture — but an estate that measures nothing is flying blind on costs that will constrain it.

ladder.description: No environmental indicator is measured; hardware has no lifecycle policy.
Basic indicators are tracked internally; disposal runs through certified channels.
Indicators are published; reuse and refurbishment are standard practice.
Reporting is independently verified; efficiency and circularity targets are tracked.
Verified reporting with demonstrated year-on-year improvement across energy, lifecycle and efficiency.

questions.text: Do you know where the estate's power comes from — the renewable share, its origin, the certificates behind it?
questions.why: Energy is a dependency like any other supply line; knowing its origin is the first step of the only sovereignty lever this objective holds.

ladder.description: The energy mix is untracked; nobody could state it today.
The provider's published figures are all you hold; nothing is institution-specific.
The mix is tracked; renewable claims rest on certificates of unknown origin.
Tracked, with EU-issued guarantees of origin covering the renewable share.
Tracked end to end: EU-generated renewable supply, verified, with contractual continuity.

questions.text: Does hardware procurement policy weigh supply-chain risk — multi-vendor sourcing, region diversification, scarce-material exposure?
questions.why: Raw-material exposure is real but unmappable in a workshop; what procurement can honestly report is whether the buying policy takes the risk seriously.

ladder.description: Procurement decides on price plus features; supply risk is not a criterion.
Supply risk is discussed for major purchases; no policy requires it.
Policy requires multi-vendor options for critical hardware categories.
Policy enforces vendor plus region diversification, with scarce-material exposure flagged where vendors disclose it.
Diversification targets are tracked, reported; single-source hardware needs an approved exception.

testEstates.name: Profile A
testEstates.description: Wholly on a non-EU hyperscaler, with an excellent programme.

testEstates.name: Profile BASE
testEstates.description: EU/open stack, EU keys, EU SOC, no foreign parent, but thin paperwork.

testEstates.name: Profile M
testEstates.description: An honest median EU public institution.
